info.name: Wallet Control Layer — Agent on a Leash
info.description:
**The control layer that decides whether an AI shopping agent may spend a customer's money.** Viseca challenge, Swiss {ai} Weeks 2026.

Every proposed purchase gets one of three answers — **approve**, **decline**, or **step_up** (ask the customer) — with a plain-language explanation and an audit record.

---

## You do not need to be a developer to use this

**Before you import this:** someone needs to have the engine running. One person on the team runs two commands:

```
make setup
make serve-live
```

…and it prints `service http://127.0.0.1:8000`. Full instructions, including what to install first, are in `postman/README.md`.

## Then

1. Pick the **Leash — local** environment (top right).
2. Open **0 · Start here** and Send the three requests.
3. Go to **2 · Watch it decide** and Send *Start a scenario*.
4. Send *See the decisions* a few times and read the **Console** at the bottom left — the decisions are printed there in plain English.

Every request explains what it does and what to look at. Requests store what the next one needs, so you never copy an ID by hand.

---

Contract: `specs/service-contract.md` · Decision semantics: `specs/decision-rules.md`

item.name: 0 · Start here
item.description: Run these three in order. If all three are green the engine is live and talking to the organizers' sandbox — you can go straight to folder 2 and watch it decide.

request.description:
Our decision service. `upstream.mode` tells you which sandbox it is pointed at:

- **live** — the organizers' API (started with `make serve-live`)
- **replica** — the offline copy on your laptop (`make serve`)

If this fails with a connection error, the server is not running. See postman/README.md.

exec: // Point folder 6 at whatever the engine is actually talking to, so the two
// can never drift apart in front of an audience.
console.log('Engine ' + b.engine_version + ' → ' + b.upstream.mode + ' sandbox at ' + b.upstream.base_url);

request.description:
Talks to the sandbox directly, bypassing our engine — the only way to tell *which* of the two is down. The UI never calls the sandbox itself.

The previous request pointed this at whatever the engine is using, so it follows you between the live sandbox and the offline replica automatically.

The decision configuration, in one response: every check that runs, the concern weights, the step-up threshold, and the five scenarios with the cardholder instruction each one enforces.

Good screen to have open while demoing.

item.name: 1 · The customer's instruction
item.description: How a sentence the cardholder typed becomes rules a machine can enforce — and how the customer keeps control of it. Run these in order; each one stores what the next needs.

request.description:
The review screen. Turns the instruction into rules **without** saving anything, so you can edit and re-run this as often as you like.

Look at `provenance` on each rule: it is the exact words of the instruction that rule came from. That is what lets a customer check the compilation instead of trusting it.

`open_questions` is what the compiler was *not* sure about. It is asked, never guessed.

exec: console.log('Rules:'); b.rules.forEach(r => console.log('  ' + r.field + ' ' + r.operator + ' ' + r.value + '   ← "' + r.provenance + '"'));
console.log('Also enforced:'); b.intent_facets.forEach(f => console.log('  ' + f.kind + '   ← "' + f.provenance + '"'));

request.description: Saves the compiled rules as a **draft** on the sandbox. A draft cannot spend anything — it is a proposal waiting for the customer.

exec: pm.test('a draft id came back', () => pm.expect(b.draft_id).to.be.a('string'));

request.description: The customer's consent. **Nothing is enforceable until this call.** The response carries the active `mandate_id`, which is what a scenario run binds to.
The stored mandate, including `guidance` and `open_questions`. Those two are **not** carried on live transaction events, so this is the only place to read them at decision time.

A mandate can always be made **stricter**: rules may be added, and `uncertainty_policy` may move approve → ask → decline.

Note: this changes the policy for *later* runs. A run in flight keeps the snapshot it started with, so nobody can move the goalposts mid-purchase.

The same call in the other direction. **This is supposed to fail with 422.**

An agent that could relax its own leash would not be a leash. A red 422 here is the test passing.

item.name: 2 · Watch it decide
item.description: Start a scenario and the engine long-polls the sandbox, decides every purchase attempt, and submits each answer — all inside the 8-second deadline. **Start here if you just want to see it work.**

request.description:
Starts scenario `{{scenario_id}}` and the loop that decides it. Returns immediately — the decisions arrive over the next few seconds.

A step-up holds a run until the customer answers — on the real platform and in the replica alike — and nobody is answering here, so `auto_resolve` declines each one for you and the run can finish. Folder 3 is where you answer one yourself.

No `mandate_id` here, so the engine compiles and confirms the scenario's own cardholder instruction for you. To use a mandate you built in folder 1, add `"mandate_id": "{{mandate_id}}"` to the body.

**Change `scenario_id` in the collection variables to try another:**

| id | what it shows |
|---|---|
| SCEN0000 | one purchase, proves the path works |
| SCEN0001 | a weekly budget that *rolls* |
| SCEN0002 | item, size and return terms |
| SCEN0003 | a hijacked-looking session, and its recovery |
| SCEN0004 | a merchant trying to manipulate the engine |

exec: console.log('run ' + b.run_id + ' started — ' + b.counters.total + ' purchase attempts incoming');
console.log('Step-ups are declined automatically here — folder 3 is where you answer one.');
console.log('Now open "See the decisions" and hit Send a few times.');

request.description:
The live picture. Hit **Send** again every second or so until `status` reads `complete`; the console below prints each decision as it lands.

`window.approved_spend_chf` is the rolling budget the engine tracks itself — the sandbox deliberately does not do this for us. Watch it go **down** as old approvals age out of the window.

exec: if (b.window.approved_spend_chf) console.log('Rolling ' + b.window.period_days + '-day spend: CHF ' + b.window.approved_spend_chf + ' (' + b.window.approvals_in_window + ' orders in the window)');
console.log('approve=' + b.counters.approve + '  decline=' + b.counters.decline + '  needs-you=' + b.counters.step_up);
// In a collection run, come back to this request until the run finishes. When
// you press Send yourself this does nothing — just press it again.

request.description: Every run this engine has started, with its counters. Useful after a demo.
Stops the loop after the decision in flight. Nothing already submitted is undone.

item.name: 3 · When it needs you
item.description: `step_up` is the third answer, and the most important one: not yes, not no — **ask the person whose money it is.** This folder runs its own scenario, so it works on its own.

item.name: Run a scenario that needs you

request.description:
SCEN0002 is the one where the cardholder asked for a specific pair of shoes, returnable within 14 days, from a sports retailer. Two of its twelve attempts are neither clearly fine nor clearly wrong — a seller who never says whether the order can be returned, and a basket with an extra item nobody asked for.

Those two become questions rather than verdicts.

The run stops at the first of them and waits for you, exactly as it would on the real platform: nothing more is decided until the customer answers.
Press Send until the run stops at a step-up — it waits there until the customer answers. Then go to the next request.

exec: console.log('It stopped to ask you — ' + b.counters.decided + ' of ' + b.counters.total + ' decided so far.');
pm.test('the run is waiting on the customer', () => pm.expect(b.status).to.eql('running'));
console.log('Finished — nothing left to ask. Run this folder again from its first request.');

item.name: What is waiting for the customer?

request.description:
The notification list. `customer_message` is exactly what the cardholder would see on their phone — plain language, no jargon, and never the merchant's own text quoted back at them.

`seconds_remaining` counts down the sandbox's 120-second confirmation window.

exec: if (!s.length) { console.log('Nothing waiting. Run this folder again from its first request.'); }
s.forEach(x => console.log('[ASK] CHF ' + x.amount_chf + ' at ' + x.merchant_name + ' — ' + x.seconds_remaining + 's left\n      ' + x.customer_message));
pm.test('the message is written for a person, not a machine', () =>

request.description:
The human answer. This is the *only* way a stepped-up payment can go through — the sandbox refuses any further automated decision on it.

Approving here also moves the amount into the rolling budget. While it was waiting it counted for nothing, which is the correct accounting: a question is not a purchase.

The run carries on the moment you answer — to its next question, or to the end.

exec: console.log('Confirmed by the customer. Rolling spend is now CHF ' + (b.window.approved_spend_chf || '0.00'));

request.description: The other answer. Run this **instead of** the previous request — a step-up can only be answered once, and a second answer is refused with 409.

exec: if (pm.response.code === 409) console.log('Already answered once — that is the rule, not a bug.');

item.name: 4 · Show your work
item.description: Every decision is written to an append-only file, one line each, and nothing is ever rewritten. This is what makes the system defensible to an issuer rather than merely clever.

request.description: The last 20 records. `type` is `decision`, `resolution` (a human answered) or `replay` (the sandbox delivered the same authorization twice).

Everything behind one decision:

- **`checks`** — all twelve, *including the ones that passed*. What else did we look at is a question with an answer.
- **`score`** — the concern arithmetic and the threshold it was measured against.
- **`enrichment`** — the history we brought to it: how often this card used this shop, whether the device is new, whether the shop's name imitates one the customer trusts.
- **`timing`** — how much of the 8-second deadline was left, and how long we took (single-digit milliseconds).
- **`upstream`** — what the *platform* did with our answer, which can differ from what we decided.
- **`inputs_digest`** — a hash of exactly what we saw, so the input cannot be disputed later.

exec: console.log('  ' + b.checks.length + ' checks ran (' + pass + ' passed), score ' + b.score.concern_score + ' vs threshold ' + b.score.step_up_threshold);
console.log('  decided in ' + b.timing.latency_ms + 'ms with ' + Math.round(b.timing.budget_ms) + 'ms of deadline left');
b.checks.filter(c => c.verdict !== 'pass' && c.detail).forEach(c => console.log('  · ' + c.verdict + ': ' + c.detail));
pm.test('every check is on the record', () => pm.expect(b.checks.length).to.eql(12));

request.description: The untouched file content for this authorization — one JSON object per line, in the order it was written. Nothing here was ever edited.
A lighter feed than the audit trail — what the UI's decision list renders.

item.name: 5 · What if the rules were different?
item.description: `/v1/decide` runs the engine over one transaction and **submits nothing**. Change the policy, re-send, and watch the answer change. This is the endpoint the UI uses for its what-if view.

request.description:
The body is a complete transaction event. This one is the organizers' own example fixture, pasted in.

Nothing is sent to the sandbox and no budget is touched, so this is safe to run as often as you like.

item.name: 6 · The organizers' sandbox (direct)
item.description: For debugging only — these bypass our engine and talk to the sandbox with the team key. Everything a demo needs is in folders 0–5.

request.description: The platform's own contract: API version, scenarios, deadline and step-up windows. Never hard-code these — read them here.

The pack the platform serves: its reference tables by name (customers, accounts, cards, merchants, items, fx_rates, scenario_catalogue) and where the history CSV lives. `make live-pack` writes this to out/live-pack.
Every runtime authorization and what the platform recorded for it. This is also what the engine reads to rebuild its state after a restart.
The append-only platform feed. Store `next_cursor` and pass it as `since`.
Wipes this team's mandates, runs and decisions so a scenario can be replayed from clean. **Disabled during judging** — expect it to fail then.

exec: pm.test('reset, or disabled during judging', () => pm.expect([200, 403, 409]).to.include(pm.response.code));
// Fail early and in plain language rather than mid-demo.
throw new Error('No environment selected. Pick "Leash — local" in the environment dropdown, top right.');
